title: Then the seer rests in itself (1.3–1.4)
hook: when the mind's whirling settles, what's left? Patanjali's answer is the one who was watching all along

segments.voice: Yesterday: atha, now. Yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Did you use the word as a fresh start today? Now the obvious question: when the turnings go still, what's left? Day four hundred thirty-one.

You're at a movie, completely absorbed. You flinch at the jump scare. You tear up at the ending. For two hours you are the story. Then the lights come up, and there you are, in a sticky seat, popcorn on your shirt, and you realize: I was here the whole time. The story was on the screen. I was the one watching. Patanjali's next two sutras are about that moment when the lights come up.
screen: `TWO HOURS INSIDE THE STORY.` → `THE LIGHTS COME UP.` → `I WAS WATCHING ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Sutra 1.3: tada drashtuh svarupe avasthanam. Then the seer rests in its own form. Tada, then: once the mind's turnings are stilled. Drashtri, the seer: in Patanjali's system, pure awareness, which he also calls purusha. Svarupa, its own form, its true nature. Avasthana, abiding, staying put. So when the whirling stops, nothing is lost. The seer is simply left as it always was. Then sutra 1.4 tells you what happens the rest of the time: otherwise, the seer seems to take on the form of the turnings. That's the movie. Anger rises in the mind, and awareness seems to become anger. A worry spins, and awareness seems to be the worry. The word seems matters. In this system, the seer never actually changes. It only looks that way, the way the moon looks broken on rippled water. Teachers often use that picture: still the ripples and the moon's reflection is whole again, though the moon itself was never in pieces. Here Patanjali leans on an older school, Samkhya, which separates two things: purusha, pure awareness, and prakriti, everything that changes, including the mind. The mind is not the seer. It's the screen. Vedanta schools describe the seer and the world in their own terms, and the Yoga Sutras keep their own. But on this point they meet: the one who sees is not the passing thoughts it sees.
screen: `TADA: THEN, WHEN THE TURNINGS STILL.` · `THE SEER RESTS IN ITS OWN FORM.` · `OTHERWISE, IT SEEMS TO BE THE TURNINGS.` · then, large: `THE MIND IS THE SCREEN.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Let thoughts come as they will. Each time one arrives, notice it the way you'd notice a scene on a screen: there's a plan. There's a memory. There's a worry. Then shift your attention, just slightly, back toward the one who is noticing. You don't have to find it or describe it. Just lean back into the seat, the way you do when the lights come up. The bell holds the time.
Drashtri, the seer, pure awareness. Sutra 1.3: when the mind's turnings are stilled, the seer abides in its own true form.

Your line: the seer. The next time a strong feeling grabs you today, add three words in your head: I see anger, I see worry, I see hurry, and notice who is doing the seeing. Day four hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: In Patanjali's yoga, practitioners learn to witness the mind's movements rather than become them, and many Hindu teachers describe meditation as resting as the witness, sakshi, behind thought.

pairs: its own form, its true nature

myth: in Patanjali's system the seer is the mind
the mind belongs to changing nature. the seer, purusha, is the awareness that sees it.
sutra 1.4 says the seer seems to take the form of the turnings
at other times, it looks as if awareness has become the thought.
the Yoga Sutras borrow ideas from the Samkhya school
the split between purusha and prakriti comes from Samkhya.

fork.setup: a wave of anger rises while you sit. according to sutra 1.4, what is happening?
options: awareness only seems to take the shape of the anger, a turning of the mind.
the anger proves the practice failed.
fork.reveal: otherwise, the seer seems to take the form of the turnings. it never really changes, the way the moon is never really broken by ripples.

original.note: Sanskrit draṣṭṛ: the seer. in the Yoga Sutras, pure awareness, also called purusha.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'the seer' is a fortune teller.
what it means: the awareness that watches every thought and is never one of them.
what a scholar hears: 1.3–1.4 apply Samkhya's split between purusha (awareness) and prakriti (nature, mind included); the seer only appears to share the form of the vrittis (vritti-sarupya).

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.3–1.4 (the seer rests in its own form; otherwise it takes the form of the turnings)
Samkhya Karika (purusha and prakriti), as background

notes: Editor review (y2 pass): the closing line no longer states as fact, in the narrator's voice, that the listener is not their thoughts; it now reports what the schools teach.
The moon on rippled water is a common teaching image, not in the sutras or Vyasa's commentary as far as the writer knows; framed as 'teachers often use'.
'Seems to' for 1.4 (vritti-sarupyam itaratra): the sutra itself has no 'seems'; the reading follows Vyasa and most commentators that purusha is unchanged. Confirm framing.
Sakshi (witness) in howItsDone is a Vedanta term; confirm it's acceptable alongside Patanjali's drashtri.
